title: Adapting Pretrained Language Models for Citation Classification via Self-Supervised Contrastive Learning

problem.claim: Citation classification identifies the intention behind academic citations for scholarly analysis.

gap.claim: Directly fine-tuning pretrained language models for citation classification is challenging because of labeled-data scarcity, contextual noise, and spurious keyphrase correlations.

contributions.claim: Citss is a framework for adapting pretrained language models to citation classification.
Citss uses self-supervised contrastive learning with sentence-level cropping and keyphrase perturbation to construct contrastive pairs and address the stated challenges.
Citss is designed to work with both encoder-based pretrained language models and decoder-based large language models.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors present Citss as a novel framework for adapting pretrained language models to citation classification.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Experiments on three benchmark datasets using encoder-based pretrained language models and decoder-based large language models reportedly outperform the previous state of the art.
The authors report that their code is available at github.com/LITONG99/Citss.

narrative_sequence.summary: Citation classification is important for scholarly analysis.
Prior work fine-tunes pretrained language models using their pretrained linguistic knowledge.
Direct fine-tuning faces labeled-data scarcity, contextual noise, and spurious keyphrase correlations.
Citss addresses these challenges through self-supervised contrastive learning, sentence-level cropping, keyphrase perturbation, and compatibility with encoder-based and decoder-based models.
Experiments across three benchmark datasets reportedly outperform the previous state of the art, and code availability is stated.

source_observation.claim: The framework targets distinct failure sources with separate contrastive-pair strategies: sentence-level cropping for long-context focus and keyphrase perturbation for reducing reliance on specific keyphrases.

interpretation.claim: Contrastive learning interventions can be aligned with identifiable data and representation problems rather than applied as a single undifferentiated technique.

application.claim: For text classification with noisy context and shortcut features, design augmentation or pair-construction strategies that separately target context focus and shortcut reliance.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether these strategies generalize beyond citation classification or which strategy drives the reported result.

unknowns: The abstract does not identify the three benchmark datasets.
Evaluation metrics, numerical results, baseline details, and statistical significance are not provided.
The abstract does not describe the contrastive-learning objective, model configurations, or training procedure.
The relative contributions of sentence-level cropping and keyphrase perturbation are not reported.
